title: The Reliability of the Bible: Historical Evidence and Eyewitness Testimony
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: Christianity as a Historical Faith
subpoints: Unlike religions based on timeless sayings or private visions, Christianity is grounded in historical events.
The faith is vulnerable to proof and open to confirmation because it relies on public, verifiable facts.
Luke writes as a historian, seeking eyewitness sources to provide an orderly account.

outline.title: The Nature of Falsifiable Faith
subpoints: The Christian faith is falsifiable because it makes propositional claims about history that can be denied.
It is also verifiable, allowing believers to respond to attacks on the faith with historical evidence.
Evidence confirms faith but does not generate it; the Bible is self-authenticating and sufficient for salvation.

outline.title: The Role of Evidence in Salvation
subpoints: Presenting more evidence does not compel an unbeliever to faith, as the natural man cannot understand the things of God.
Unbelievers suppress the truth in unrighteousness despite the clarity of the evidence.
Preaching of Christ saves, not the accumulation of external proofs.

outline.title: Eyewitness Claims in the Gospels
subpoints: The Gospels provide internal evidence that authors were eyewitnesses or had access to them.
John explicitly claims to be a witness to the events he recorded.
The testimony of the disciples is presented as true and reliable.

summary:
In this session, Pastor Tito Lyro continues the series on the reliability of the Bible by examining the historical nature of the Christian faith. He distinguishes Christianity from religions based on timeless sayings or private visions, emphasizing that the faith is grounded in specific historical events, particularly the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus. This historical basis makes the faith both falsifiable and verifiable, allowing it to be tested against the known facts of the ancient world. The pastor highlights Luke’s method as a historian, who sought out eyewitnesses to provide an orderly and certain account for Theophilus.

The discussion addresses the logical concept of falsifiability, noting that while the faith can be challenged by attacking its historical facts, it is also supported by verifiable evidence. However, it is clarified that while evidence confirms the faith for believers, it does not compel unbelievers to believe. The natural man is unable to understand spiritual truths, and the suppression of truth in unrighteousness means that the preaching of Christ, rather than external evidence, is the means of salvation.

Finally, the sermon turns to the internal evidence within the Gospels themselves. The text points to the explicit claims of the authors, such as John, who identifies himself as an eyewitness to the events recorded. These testimonies serve as foundational proof that the biblical narratives are rooted in the direct experiences of those who lived them, reinforcing the reliability of the Scriptures as historical documents.
